lead: Periodic noise is interference from a machine or a cable, not random grain. It adds a repeating stripe or grid to the image. In the Fourier spectrum, a pure sinusoid becomes a pair of bright points away from the centre. A notch filter deletes those points and leaves the rest. Use it on scanner lines, power-supply hum and camera readout patterns.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for the degradation model, 3.2 for why periodic noise is not covered by the PDF models, and Unit 2, Filtering in the frequency domain, for the DFT and masks.

sections.h3: From interference to two spectral spikes

blocks.text: Periodic noise is a repeating pattern added during capture. A scanner clock, a motor, a power supply or a camera readout can inject a sinusoid into every row or column. In the space domain you see stripes or a grid. In the frequency domain you see two bright points.

blocks.where: n is the added noise; A is its amplitude; x and y are pixel indices; N and M are the image width and height in pixels; (u₀,v₀) is the interference frequency in cycles per image; φ is phase.

blocks.text: The DFT of a real image satisfies F(u,v) = F*(N−u, M−v), with indices taken modulo N and M. F* is the complex conjugate. So a real sinusoid gives a conjugate pair at (u₀,v₀) and (N−u₀, M−v₀).

Vertical stripes vary along x, so v₀ = 0. If the stripe period is T pixels, u₀ = N/T. The two spikes sit on the u-axis. Random noise spreads over the whole spectrum; periodic noise concentrates. That is why a tiny mask can remove it without blurring the whole image.
Work in unshifted DFT coordinates u = 0…N−1 and v = 0…M−1. Let D₀ be the notch radius in frequency bins. Define the distance to the first spike and to its partner:

blocks.where: D₁ is the distance from frequency point (u,v) to the spike at (u₀,v₀); D₂ is the distance to the partner at (N−u₀, M−v₀); all distances are in frequency bins.

blocks.text: Build one high-pass factor for each notch and multiply: H(u,v) = H₁(u,v) H₂(u,v). At D_k = 0 the factor is 0; far from both notches H ≈ 1.

items: Ideal: H<sub>k</sub> = 0 if D<sub>k</sub> ≤ D₀, else 1. Hard edge, so it can ring.
Butterworth of order n: H<sub>k</sub> = 1 / [1 + (D₀/D<sub>k</sub>)<sup>2n</sup>]. Smooth transition.
Gaussian: H<sub>k</sub> = 1 − exp(−D<sub>k</sub>²/(2D₀²)). Smooth, less ringing.
Notch pass: H<sub>pass</sub> = 1 − H<sub>reject</sub>. It keeps the interference and removes the rest; use it only to inspect the noise.
Band-reject removes a ring of radii; band-pass is its complement. A notch is the limiting case of a very narrow band-reject.

blocks.text: Work on the unshifted DFT. The display can be shifted, but the mask coordinates and the array you multiply must use the same origin.

items: Compute F = DFT of the noisy image g.
Compute L = log(1 + |F|) and display it centred with fftshift. The spikes become visible.
Read each spike coordinate in unshifted indices. For (u₀,v₀), add the partner (N−u₀, M−v₀).
Choose D₀, usually 1–3 bins, and a filter type. Build H with notches at both points.
Multiply the complex spectrum: F ← F · H.
Take the inverse DFT, keep the real part, and clip to 0–255 for 8-bit display.

blocks.text: The log magnitude is only a viewing aid. Do not multiply the log by H; multiply the complex F. After the inverse DFT, round-off leaves a tiny imaginary part; discard it. Keep D₀ small. A wide notch removes real image frequencies near the spike and blurs edges. A narrow notch can leave a faint residual stripe.

figure.caption: The log spectrum shows two spikes; the mask zeroes that pair and leaves the centre and the rest of the spectrum. The inverse DFT returns a clean image.

spec.title: Notch filtering
spec.aria: A chain from the noisy image through the DFT, the log spectrum with two spikes, the notch mask, the inverse DFT and the clean image.

examples.question: A 256×256 image has vertical stripes with a period of T = 8 pixels. (a) Find the interference frequency u₀. (b) Give both spike locations in the DFT. (c) State a suitable notch radius D₀. (d) Find the distance between the two spikes and explain why notching only one fails.
steps: N = 256 pixels and T = 8 pixels, so u₀ = N/T = 256/8 = 32 cycles per image width.
Vertical stripes vary along x, so v₀ = 0. The first spike is at (u,v) = (32,0).
A notch radius D₀ = 2 bins is enough for a clean spike on a 256×256 image.
Distance between spikes = |224−32| = 192 bins along the u-axis.
A notch of radius 2 at (32,0) has H ≈ 1 at (224,0) because D = 192 is far greater than 2. The partner survives, so the residual sinusoid is still visible. Mask both points.
examples.answer: u₀ = 32 cycles per image width; spikes at (32,0) and (224,0); D₀ = 2 bins; separation 192 bins, so both spikes must be notched.
examples.check:
N = 256
T = 8
u0 = N // T
partner = N - u0
D0 = 2
dist = abs(partner - u0)
print(u0)
print(partner)
print(D0)
print(dist)

traps: Notching a single spike and forgetting the conjugate partner. A real image has a symmetric DFT, so half the sinusoid remains.
Notching the origin (0,0). That removes the DC term; the inverse DFT has zero mean and the image turns mid-grey.
Using fftshifted coordinates in an unshifted mask, or the reverse. The notch lands in the wrong place and the stripe survives.
Making D₀ too large. Real image frequencies near the spike are removed and the restored image blurs.
Confusing notch reject with notch pass. Reject removes the interference; pass keeps it and is only for inspection.

quiz.q: What does a pure sinusoid look like in the magnitude spectrum of a real image?
quiz.a: Two impulse-like spikes: one at (u₀,v₀) and its conjugate partner at (N−u₀, M−v₀).

quiz.q: Why must notches be placed in pairs for a real image?
quiz.a: The DFT of a real image is conjugate symmetric. A real sinusoid has a positive-frequency spike and a negative-frequency spike, so removing one leaves the other.

quiz.q: A 512×512 image has vertical stripes with period T = 16 pixels. Find u₀ and the partner spike.
An ideal notch has D₀ = 3 bins and its first centre at (64,0). What is H(66,0)?
Why can an ideal notch produce ringing while a Gaussian notch usually does not?
quiz.a: The ideal mask jumps sharply between 0 and 1 in frequency. Its inverse DFT is sinc-like and spreads ripples in space. The Gaussian mask is smooth, so its inverse has much weaker ringing.

quiz.q: A student places a notch at (0,0). What happens to the image and why?
quiz.a: The DC term is removed. The inverse DFT then has zero mean, so the image becomes mid-grey and loses contrast.

quiz.q: What is a notch pass filter used for?
quiz.a: H<sub>pass</sub> = 1 − H<sub>reject</sub>. It keeps the periodic noise and removes the rest, so it is used to inspect or measure the interference, not to restore the image.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production, periodic noise removal is often done with flat-field or dark-frame calibration before notch filtering. Modern scanners cancel clock harmonics in firmware. Video can carry a fixed pattern, so engineers estimate the frequency with a periodogram and then apply an adaptive notch. Search for periodogram, notch filter, fixed-pattern noise and flat-field correction.
